entities.summary:
Demetrius (c. 215 BCE – 180 BCE) was a pivotal figure in the tumultuous politics of Hellenistic Macedon, whose life and death significantly influenced the trajectory of the Antigonid kingdom's relationship with the ascendant Roman Republic. As the younger son of King Philip V, Demetrius spent critical years as a hostage in Rome following the Second Macedonian War (200–197 BCE), a period that exposed him to Roman culture and political machinations, and crucially, fostered a pro-Roman stance that would ultimately prove fatal. His perceived favor with the Romans, cultivated during his time in the Republic, positioned him as a potential successor in the eyes of the Roman Senate, a prospect that deeply alarmed his elder brother, Perseus, and his father, Philip V.

Upon his return to Macedon in 187 BCE, Demetrius became an unwitting pawn in the escalating tensions between Macedon and Rome. His diplomatic missions to Rome in 184 and 183 BCE, ostensibly to defend Macedonian interests against accusations from neighboring Greek states, further solidified his image as a Roman sympathizer. This perception was masterfully exploited by Perseus, who, fearing Demetrius's influence and potential Roman backing for the throne, fabricated evidence of Demetrius's treasonous correspondence with Roman officials. Perseus's accusations, which included forged letters and false testimonies, convinced Philip V that Demetrius was plotting to usurp the throne with Roman assistance. This deep-seated suspicion, fueled by Macedonian anti-Roman sentiment and the king's own declining health, led to Demetrius's tragic downfall.
